Further, texture can be used to deduce water erodibility (Boden, 2005; FAO, 2006). Common are silty clay loams (SiCL), silt loams (SiL), loams (L), sand loams (SL) and loam sands (LS) (FAO, 2006: 27), whereby silt loams are “highly erodible” (k-factor of 0.3–0.5) and loams (L), both sandy and clayey forms, are “moderately erodible”

1 (Ap to 14C horizons) and Ir02 (C to 9C horizons). To clarify this fact, contents of coarse sand (2000–630 μm) and ﬁne silt (6.3–2 μm) were listed in Fig. 5. Deduced from texture, the erodibility of silty and loamy terrace soils is high to very high (k-factor of >0.3), except for loamy sands, which are moderately erodible (according to Ad-Hoc-AG Boden, 2005). Silt loams in Wadi Al-Jidar account for 30%, loams for 55% and sand loams for 15% (n=39). While the contents of coarse sand ranging from 1 to 38% are highly variable when looking at layers/ horizons of both proﬁles, ﬁne silt contents differ signiﬁcantly between the proﬁles: Mean silt content in Ir01 is only 5.7% (n=19) and in Ir02 it is11.6% (n=14). Clay contents range from 7% (Jid-Cs) and 16 to 25% (Apb horizons of Ir01, Ir02 and Ir15), whereas the older and thicker ApbBw horizons of Ir02 and Ir15 had higher clay contents than shallow Apb horizons in the young proﬁle Ir01 (Table 3).
